# Discussion

This study evaluated box-score player value indices against regularised adjusted plus-minus in nine EuroLeague seasons. PIR and a related composite depended strongly on player role, even among players with the same on-court impact, whereas RAPM did not; RAPM predicted future lineup performance better; and lineups selected by integer programming, whichever value they maximised, showed no advantage over the five players coaches had used most.

The role dependence of box-score indices follows from their construction. Rebounds, blocks, high-percentage shots near the rim and fouls drawn are concentrated in interior roles, whereas the contributions of floor-spacing and off-ball players — creating space, drawing defenders, making the extra pass — leave little trace in the box score. RAPM, by contrast, credits players with what happens to the score while they are on court, adjusted for teammates and opponents [@grassetti2020extended]. Three checks indicate that the difference is not an artefact: role effects on PIR remained when RAPM was held constant, when roles were defined without PIR components, and when the lower reliability of RAPM was taken into account. In practice, PIR-type indices should not be used to compare players across roles, for example in scouting or contract decisions, without role-specific reference values.

The predictive comparison points in the same direction but is less conclusive within seasons. Out of time, RAPM explained more of the variance in future lineup net rating than summed PIR or VAL, with confidence intervals that excluded zero. Within seasons, RAPM-based lineup value was the only measure clearly associated with second-half performance, but paired comparisons could not distinguish it from box-score values or from the coach's allocation of minutes. Box-score indices thus appear to add little to what coaches already reveal through playing time.

Optimised lineups showed no advantage over the players coaches used most, and they shared about three of their five players with the coach's choice. Three factors can explain this. First, coaches observe information that box scores do not record, including defence, matchups, health and practice performance, so their rotations already favour the best players. Second, maximising estimated values selects players whose estimates are inflated by noise, so realised performance falls short of the estimate — the optimiser's curse [@smith2006optimizer]. Third, segment outcomes are noisy and optimised fives rarely play together exactly. Optimisation approaches to team building [@muniz2022sports] should therefore report the coach benchmark; outperforming the team average is not sufficient evidence of added value.

## Limitations

All analyses relied on segment-level net rating, which is very noisy. The confidence intervals of the lineup comparisons spanned about ±4–5 points per 100 possessions, so moderate advantages or disadvantages of optimisation cannot be excluded; the result is an absence of evidence of benefit rather than evidence of equivalence. RAPM is itself estimated with error and penalisation, and it was used both as a value measure and to adjust for opponents; its out-of-time advantage, however, does not presuppose that RAPM is correct, because it is judged against observed outcomes. RAPM drew on all prior seasons, whereas the first-half box-score values did not; box-score values pooled over the same period gave similar results. Box-score values could not be computed for low-minute players, but the conclusions were unchanged in the subset of segments in which all measures were defined. Optimised fives were observed only when coaches happened to field most of them, which limits the precision of the comparison; because the coach benchmark was evaluated in the same way, the comparison is not biased in either direction. Lineup optimisation used season-half information and did not model fatigue, fouls or matchups, which coaches manage in real time. Finally, the results concern the EuroLeague; because data and code are open, they can be tested in other leagues.

## Conclusions

Box-score indices such as PIR rate interior roles higher than players with the same on-court impact in other roles, and lineups optimised on these or on plus-minus values showed no advantage over coaches' own rotations. Clubs and analysts can therefore use plus-minus-based values when comparing players across roles, and should evaluate any lineup decision tool against the coach's most-used players rather than against the team average.
